newsitem.title: USA: Common infection may become untreatable, CDC says.
newsitem.headline: Common infection may become untreatable, CDC says.

text.p: A microorganism that is a common cause of hospital infections has developed resistance to the only antibiotic that remained effective against it, U.S. health experts said on Wednesday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the first cases of vancomycin-resistant staphylococcus aureus have been reported in Japan. In one hospital, a young patient remained infected after 29 days of treatment with vancomycin.

"This is really our first report of a failure to treat one of these organisms with vancomycin and that's a concern for us," the CDC's Fred Tenover said. "We need to be aware of the fact that these organisms are now present and we need to start looking for them in U.S. hospitals."

Tenover said six other Japanese hospitals have reported "increased resistance" by the microorganism. "It is the first time that we've seen these type of organisms express any level of resistance," he said.

The drug vancomycin has been successfully used for more than three decades, but beginning in 1989, there was a rapid increase in vancomycin-resistant enterococci, another common source of infection in hospitals. Since then, scientists have been concerned that the vancomycin-resistance genes in enterococci might be transferred to staphylococcus aureus.
"It doesn't have the high level of resistance that we see in the enterococci, nonetheless it is a concern because this patient did not respond to therapy," Tenover said.
The CDC is developing specific guidelines to prevent the spread of vancomycin-resistant staphylococcus aureus. They will probably be issued in August.

Tenover, of the CDC's hospital infections branch, said vancomycin was the antiobiotic of last resort against the microorganism. Staphylococcus aureus is already resistant to penicillin and methicillin.

He said pharmaceutical companies have shifted away from antibiotic production and toward anti-viral and anti-fungal drugs. "The prudent use of the antibiotics we have now is of utmost importance," Tenover said.
A team of researchers wrote last year in the Annals of Internal Medicine that the emergence of vancomycin-resistant staphylococcus aureus could "set infectious diseases back 60 years."
Staphylococcus is particularly troublesome in hospitals since it can be transmitted when health care workers' hands become infected through contact with patients or body fluids.
Hospital workers are encouraged to wash their hands and wear gloves, masks and gowns to reduce transmission of infections. They are also asked to carefully handle devices and laundry.
